In parts of Australia’s interior, a year can bring less than 250 millimeters of rain. What turns a green, crowded shoreline into a continent-sized red dryland?

[curious, intimate] Follow the water.

Pacific air, carried inland by easterly winds, meets the Great Dividing Range, a chain of highlands paralleling the east coast. Forced uphill, it cools; moisture condenses and falls as rain on the eastern slopes. Descending westward, the air warms and dries. The range casts a rain shadow—but it is only part of the story. Much of inland Australia lies beneath subtropical high pressure, where sinking air discourages clouds, and far from ocean moisture.

[PAUSE]

That combination is the continent’s great bottleneck: water is scarce before it can travel deep inland.

Beyond the range, rivers often run only after rare downpours. Heat quickly evaporates surface water; plants grow slowly, and iron-rich minerals give the landscape its famous red color. This is not one endless dune field. It is a vast mosaic of stony deserts, scrub, and dry grassland—beautiful, but hard to farm or support dense settlement.

[serious] And it is not literally empty: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived across these lands for tens of thousands of years, with communities shaped by local water and country.

[with growing energy] The contrast is striking: Australia’s population clusters in a narrow band of temperate, well-watered coastal cities, especially in the east and southeast. Sydney, Brisbane, and Melbourne grew where ports, reliable supplies, and productive land meet. Cross the mountains, and settlements become far apart, linked by long roads across immense distances.

One landmark makes that divide visible. The Dingo Fence stretches about 5,600 kilometers across the southeast, built to keep dingoes away from sheep country. The fence is longer than the distance from New York to Los Angeles. It is no wall between people and wilderness, but a reminder that Australia’s most valuable pasture lies on the wetter side—and protecting it takes a monumental barrier.

So why is 90 percent of Australia called empty? Not because nothing lives there. The rain-bearing air loses much of its water at the coast and mountains, while the interior’s climate keeps the rest scarce. People, farms, and cities gather where water stays. The red center remains immense, inhabited, and thinly populated.

deepseek-v4-flash.text: Australia has a fence so long it could stretch from New York to Los Angeles and keep going. It runs 5,600 kilometers—longer than the U.S.-Mexico border. And it wasn't built to stop people. It was built to stop dingoes. That fence marks the sharpest divide on Earth: the green, crowded coast on one side; the empty red desert on the other. Why is this line so brutal? Because of a mountain range called the Great Dividing Range. [curious, intimate] Look at a satellite map of Australia from space. You see a narrow strip of green along the southeast coast—then nothing but ochre for thousands of kilometers. That strip holds nearly all of Australia's 27 million people. The rest of the continent? Almost nobody. Here's the mechanism. The Pacific Ocean sends moisture-laden winds westward. They hit the Great Dividing Range, rise, cool, and drop their rain onto the coastal slopes. Sydney gets over a meter of rain per year. Then the air crosses the mountain crest and plunges down the far side, compressing and warming. [with growing energy] That hot, dry air sucks every drop of available moisture out of the soil. The rain shadow effect—a mountain-sized wall that turns half a continent into desert. [PAUSE] Travel just a few hundred kilometers inland, and rainfall collapses to under 250 millimeters a year. Too dry for crops. Too dry for towns. Too dry for people. That's why the eastern coast is a cramped ribbon of cities—and why the interior is the emptiest place on any inhabited continent. [serious] And that's where the Dingo Fence comes in. For thousands of kilometers, it runs along the edge of this desolation, protecting sheep and cattle from Australia's native wild dog. But really, it's a symbol: beyond this fence, the rain shadow has already won. Australia's emptiness isn't due to bad luck or policy. It's due to a simple, relentless fact: a mountain range steals the rain from an entire nation. [PAUSE] The fence doesn't keep people out. The rain shadow does.
